vignette:
He walks into the consulting room and takes the same seat he has taken every session for the past eight weeks-the one with the wall directly behind him. He does this without looking, as if his body still remembers the geometry of danger. He is a forty-eight-year-old Middle Eastern man, a fashion designer. I know this before he speaks because of how he sits: upright, precise, as if being observed. His PCL-5 score was thirty-four when he first came to see me. The number is a shorthand for a weight I am only beginning to understand.

He tells the story in pieces, the way fabric is unrolled from a bolt-slowly, carefully, afraid of what might spill out. Before the disaster, he was a different man. He had a reputation for architectural lines, for structure that celebrated the body. He was married. He lived in a city with ancient souks and runways, where he sourced the best silks. He describes it as a world of order, of deliberate beauty.

The disaster was a bombing. He was at a textile fair in the old souk, two years ago. He was reaching for a bolt of pale silk for his Fall collection when the first bomb struck the entrance. He remembers the sound not as a bang but as a pressure, a sudden weight of air. Then the ceiling fell. He was pinned for six hours. He lay in the dark next to a young woman from another studio. He held her hand. She wore heavy jasmine and sandalwood. He listened to her breathing for a long time, and then he listened to the silence. He does not talk about what happened to her. He does not have to.

He was rescued. His body healed. But he stopped sleeping. He stopped feeling like a husband. He looked at his wife and saw only the dust on her clothes from the hospital, the fear in her eyes reflected back at him. He felt like a piece of shrapnel inside the house, sharp and dangerous. He started to rage at small things-the way she set the table, the sound of her footsteps. Then he stopped speaking altogether. He divorced her a year later. He tells me he did it to set her free, and he believes this deeply, even as his voice cracks.

Now he works in a quiet city. He lives alone in a ground-floor apartment with thick curtains. He wakes every morning at exactly 4:51 AM, the time the first wall fell, and he does not try to go back to sleep. He goes to his studio in the dark. He is a ghost there. His latest collection is entirely monochrome. Color, he says, feels like a demand. It is too loud.

His hands, which once sculpted fabric, now tremble over a bolt of silk. He cannot buy new materials. The textures betray him-crushed velvet feels like clots of blood, linen like the dust of crushed concrete. Last week, a client arrived wearing jasmine and sandalwood perfume. He had to excuse himself and vomited in the bathroom. The shame of that moment sits in the room with us as he recounts it. He pulls at the skin around his cuticles. He uncrosses and recrosses his legs. He cannot stand still.

He tells me his mind feels like a poorly stitched seam-everything is coming apart. He cannot draw a new line without seeing a crack in a ceiling. He cannot feel joy. He feels only a flat, grey vigilance. He checks the exits, the windows, the faces of strangers. He spends his days exhausted but terrified of rest.

At the end of this session, he pauses at the door. He tells me he ordered the silk. The same pale silk he was reaching for that morning. It arrived three days ago. He has not opened the box. It sits on his cutting table. He wanted me to know. He says this without looking back, his hand on the doorframe. Then he leaves. The room feels very quiet.
